segments.source_text: أما أشهر أعماله الطبية فهو «القانون في الطب». قسمه إلى خمسة كتب تناولت مبادئ الطب، والأدوية المفردة، وأمراض أعضاء الجسم، والأمراض اللي بتصيب أكتر من عضو، والأدوية المركبة. وكان بيعرض المعرفة الطبية المتاحة في عصره وينظمها في مرجع واحد. وترتيب الأبواب الخمسة خلّى القارئ ينتقل من المبادئ العامة إلى موضوعات أكثر تحديدًا، بدل ما يواجه معلومات متفرقة من غير تنظيم. وده كان مهمًا في زمن كانت فيه الكتب الطبية بتجمع خبرات ومعارف تراكمت عبر أجيال.

segments.source_text: وفي النصف الثاني من القرن الثاني عشر، ترجم جيرارد الكريموني الكتاب من العربية إلى اللاتينية في مدينة طليطلة. وبعدها انتشر في أوروبا، وأصبح جزءًا من تعليم الطب في جامعات ومراكز علمية، وظل يُدرَّس حتى أواخر القرن السابع عشر. وده يوضح قد إيه أثر الكتاب امتد بعيدًا عن العالم اللي عاش فيه ابن سينا. وانتقال الكتاب من العربية إلى اللاتينية فتح له طريقًا جديدًا للوصول إلى قراء ومدرسين في بيئات لغوية مختلفة. ومع تداول نسخه وشرحه، أصبح جزءًا من تاريخ انتقال المعرفة الطبية بين مناطق وثقافات متعددة.

segments.speaker: karma
segments.source_text: When I learn about scholars from long ago, I’m struck by how some people who lived more than a thousand years ago still have books and ideas that shape the history of medicine and philosophy we study today.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.source_text: One of these scholars was Abu Ali al-Husayn ibn Abd Allah ibn Sina, known as Ibn Sina. He was born around 980 CE in the village of Afshana, near Bukhara, in the region that is now Uzbekistan. In the Islamic world he became known by the title “al-Shaykh al-Ra’is,” and in Europe he was known as “Avicenna.” At that time, Bukhara was an important center of learning and culture in the region, giving him access to an environment shaped by books, scholarship, and intellectual exchange.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.source_text: His family moved to Bukhara when he was young. There, he studied different subjects, including Islamic jurisprudence and medicine. Over time, his interests expanded to include philosophy, logic, and the natural sciences.

segments.speaker: karma
segments.source_text: His interests clearly went beyond medicine. He wanted to understand the human body and also think deeply about knowledge and the natural world. This shows how broad his thinking was: he did not separate the study of the human body from the effort to understand the wider world.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.source_text: This range of interests can be seen in his writings. Ibn Sina wrote about medicine, but he also explored philosophy, logic, and the natural sciences. One of his best-known works is The Book of Healing, or al-Shifa. Despite its name, it is not a medical treatment book; it is a major encyclopedia covering logic, mathematics, the natural sciences, philosophy, and metaphysics. The work brings together a wide range of philosophical and scientific subjects, showing that his intellectual interests reached far beyond a single field.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.source_text: His best-known medical work is The Canon of Medicine. He divided it into five books covering the principles of medicine, simple drugs, diseases of individual organs, diseases affecting more than one organ, and compound medicines. It presented and organized the medical knowledge available in his time in a single reference work. The arrangement of the five books guided readers from general principles to more specific subjects instead of leaving the information scattered. This organization mattered in an age when medical books brought together knowledge and experience accumulated over generations.

segments.speaker: karma
segments.source_text: What stands out is that the book was not simply a collection of information. It was arranged so that doctors and students could find the subject they needed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.source_text: Readers could look up a particular topic, whether it concerned the human body, symptoms of an illness, a medicine, or a treatment method known at the time. They could use its sections to return to a particular medical subject they were studying.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.source_text: In the second half of the twelfth century, Gerard of Cremona translated the book from Arabic into Latin in the city of Toledo. It then spread through Europe, became part of medical teaching at universities and scholarly centers, and continued to be taught until the late seventeenth century. This shows how far the book’s influence reached beyond the world in which Ibn Sina lived. The move from Arabic into Latin opened a new path for the book to reach readers and teachers in different linguistic settings. As copies circulated and the work was studied, it became part of the history of medical knowledge moving between regions and cultures.

segments.speaker: karma
segments.source_text: Although the book was an important reference in its time, that does not mean its treatments remain suitable for every age. Medical knowledge changes as new research and evidence emerge.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.source_text: This is an important difference between studying the history of medicine and practicing medicine today. Ibn Sina’s book helps us understand the medical knowledge of his time, but not every old explanation or treatment is suitable today. Modern medicine relies on research, experiments, and new evidence.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.source_text: That is why we study old medical books as part of the history of science, not as a replacement for a doctor or an approved treatment. Any medical advice should be based on current evidence and assessment by a qualified professional.

segments.speaker: narrator

L’ouvrage présentait et organisait en une seule référence les connaissances médicales disponibles à son époque. L’organisation en cinq livres guidait le lecteur des principes généraux vers des sujets plus précis, au lieu de laisser les informations dispersées. segments.source_text: Dans la seconde moitié du XIIe siècle, Gérard de Crémone traduisit le livre de l’arabe vers le latin dans la ville de Tolède. Il se diffusa ensuite en Europe, entra dans l’enseignement de la médecine dans des universités et des centres savants, et resta étudié jusqu’à la fin du XVIIe siècle. Cela montre jusqu’où son influence s’est étendue, bien au-delà du monde où vivait Ibn Sina. Le passage de l’arabe au latin a ouvert à l’ouvrage une nouvelle voie vers des lecteurs et des enseignants de langues différentes. À mesure que les copies circulaient et que le livre était étudié, il est devenu un élément de l’histoire de la transmission des connaissances médicales entre régions et cultures.
